nameStory: The Purple Jellydisc gets its name from its striking appearance - clusters of gelatinous, disc-shaped fungi that range from pinkish to deep purple in color. The jelly-like texture is so pronounced that it's also commonly called "jelly drops," perfectly describing how these squishy fungi look like colorful drops of jelly scattered across dead wood.
description: Purple Jellydisc is a fascinating fungus that forms clusters of soft, gelatinous discs on dead wood throughout New England's forests. These eye-catching fungi appear as small, rounded cushions or shallow cups with a distinctly jelly-like consistency and beautiful purple to pinkish coloration. Unlike mushrooms with stems and caps, these fungi grow directly from the wood surface in tight groups. They're quite small, typically forming masses just a few inches across, but their vibrant color makes them surprisingly noticeable against dark bark.

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: Feels exactly like firm jelly or gelatin when touched - soft, bouncy, and slightly sticky but not slimy. You can gently press them and they'll spring back into shape.

idTips.label: Purple-pink color
idTips.description: Ranges from bright pinkish-purple to deep violet, sometimes with translucent edges. The color is quite vivid and doesn't fade much even when the fungi dry out slightly.

idTips.label: Disc-shaped growth
idTips.description: Forms small, flattened discs or shallow cups rather than typical mushroom shapes. Individual discs are usually less than an inch across but cluster together densely.

idTips.label: Dead wood habitat
idTips.description: Always grows directly from dead branches, logs, or stumps - never on living trees or on the ground. Look for them erupting right from the bark surface.

idTips.label: Clustered growth pattern
idTips.description: Appears in tight groups of dozens of individual discs, creating colorful patches several inches wide. Rarely found as single, isolated specimens.

habitat: Purple Jellydisc thrives on dead hardwood and softwood branches and logs throughout New England's mixed forests. You'll find them from sea level to mountain elevations, particularly common on fallen branches of oak, maple, birch, and spruce trees. They prefer partially shaded forest floors where dead wood retains some moisture but isn't completely waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Fresh, vibrant clusters emerge on dead wood as temperatures warm and moisture increases. This is peak season for finding the most colorful, jelly-like specimens.
seasonality.summer: Continues to fruit actively, especially after rain periods. Hot, dry spells may cause them to shrink and darken temporarily.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing and easily spotted. Autumn rains often trigger new flushes of bright purple discs on recently fallen branches.
seasonality.winter: May persist in a dried, darkened state but becomes less conspicuous. Fresh growth is rare but possible during warm spells.

funFact: Purple Jellydisc actually produces its own natural antibiotic called ascocorynin that can kill certain bacteria - essentially, this colorful forest fungus is manufacturing its own medicine right there on the log!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other jelly fungi like Witch's Butter, but Purple Jellydisc's distinctive purple color and disc shape make it fairly unique. Remember: purple discs on dead wood, not the bright yellow or orange colors of other jelly fungi.
contextualKnowledge: This fungus has a complex identity crisis in the scientific world because it can reproduce both sexually and asexually, leading to different forms that were once thought to be separate species. Don't worry though - in the field, the purple jelly discs are unmistakable regardless of their reproductive mood!
compareHints: Purple Jellydisc differs from its close relative Ascocoryne cylichnium primarily in color - cylichnium tends to be more whitish or pale rather than the distinctive purple-pink of sarcoides. Both have the same jelly-like texture and grow on dead wood, but the vibrant purple color is your best clue you've found the Purple Jellydisc rather than its paler cousin.
